title: What Is an Embedded Integration Platform and How It Works
summary: An embedded integration platform enables software developers to build native third-party connections without maintaining complex backend infrastructure.
body_markdown:
## How embedded integration architecture functions behind the scenes


### The connector library and authentication layer


Embedded integration platforms function by abstracting the complex authentication handshakes and API schemas of third-party services into a standardized internal format.


The connector library acts as the translator between your application and external tools like Zendesk or HubSpot.


When a customer connects their account, the platform manages the OAuth 2.0 flows and refreshes tokens automatically. Your engineering team doesn't have to build custom logic for every provider's unique expiration policy.


### Programmatic control via integration APIs and sdks


The host application communicates with the embedded platform through a specialized Integration API or client-side SDK. This mechanism allows your app to programmatically tell the platform which user is currently active and which specific workflow template should be triggered.


When a user clicks "Enable Sync" in your UI, your backend sends a request to the platform's API containing the user's unique identifier and the desired configuration parameters.


The SDK then initializes the connection, ensuring the platform knows exactly which data silo to access without the user ever seeing a technical setup screen.


### Workflow engines and execution logs


The workflow engine is the orchestration heart that triggers actions based on specific events, such as a new lead appearing in a CRM. It processes the logic: the branching, loops, and data mapping.


It also generates execution logs that serve as the audit trail for every transaction.


These logs are critical for support teams. They provide the exact payload sent to a destination like Slack, allowing you to troubleshoot a failed sync without guessing what data caused the error.


### Choosing between unified APIs and workflow engines


Architectural choices for embedded platforms generally fall into two categories: Unified APIs or Workflow Engines. A Unified API provides a single, standardized schema for an entire category of software, such as CRMs or HRIS platforms.


This approach is entirely headless, meaning your developers build the user interface and the logic, while the platform simply normalizes the data coming from different vendors.


A Unified API allows a developer to write a single integration against the platform's "Universal CRM" schema, which the platform then maps to the specific APIs of Salesforce, HubSpot, and others.


This abstraction means you code the logic once and it works for every supported vendor in that category.


A Workflow Engine, by contrast, provides both the execution logic and a visual interface that can be embedded into your product. This allows your end-users to build their own custom automations using a drag-and-drop builder.


While a Unified API is ideal for simple data syncing, a Workflow Engine is necessary when your customers need to define their own business rules and multi-step processes.


### The embedded builder vs. headless API integration


Choosing between a visual builder and a headless API approach determines whether your end-users manage their own automation or if your developers must hard-code every workflow.

While IFrames allow for the fastest deployment, they often create a "box within a box" feel.


Conversely, using an SDK with pre-built components allows you to offer a white-labeled experience while still leveraging the platform's underlying logic.


For teams using advanced AI to assist in mapping, you can integrate models like Gemini 3.8 Flash or GPT-6 Astra via the API-only path to suggest field mappings based on historical log data.
